newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE--EMU to aid Europe's fledgling muni market.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE--EMU to aid Europe's fledgling muni market.

text.p: Europe's great towns and cities have a wealth of history and tradition but they are poor at attracting funds from international investors. EMU might help.
City and regional government bond issues now are sporadic, terms often vary widely, and there is no European market with the same depth of interest and homogeneity as the U.S. municipal bond market.
But analysts believe a single European currency could change all that, even if it won't remove all the practical and cultural obstacles.

"Given the cloak of a single currency, there's a chance that (a European muni bond market) could happen," said John Langton, chief executive of the International Securities Market Association (ISMA) in Zurich.
"The market needs that. The sort of funding that's been done at a local level could certainly be done on an international basis."
TAXING MATTERS
The first, and most important, issue to resolve is tax.

The muni bond market in the U.S. has thrived on the tax breaks investors receive. Aside from gaining a sense of civic pride, U.S. muni bond investors avoid paying various taxes in return for funding local projects.
But in Europe, tax regimes vary as widely as the cultures.

"My gut feeling is that if the single currency goes ahead -- I still say if, I don't think it's a given -- then the second phase would mean far closer consolidation of all tax and fiscal policies," Langton said.

Mark Fox, chief European strategist at Lehman Brothers in London, said the impact from European economic and monetary union (EMU) on muni bond markets in Europe would be modest unless tax matters became a priority.
"Yes EMU will help the muni market grow. But no, it will get to nowhere like the U.S. unless tax breaks are introduced."
So far, moves towards European muni issuance have been patchy, but they are gaining momentum.

In March, Italy authorised city administrations to issue bonds abroad in foreign currencies. Italrating, an Italian credit agency, in July said there were some 240 potential issuers which could tap the market.

Rome launched 100 billion lire of munibonds in July to pay for a fleet of new trams to improve its transport service. In the same month, Milan said it would issue a foreign currency bond valued at 150 billion lire to help pay for projects such as renovating La Scala, the renowned opera house.
EUROPE VS THE U.S.
Michael Maguire, managing director of bond guarantors MBIA/AMBAC International in Armonk, New York, said that in the U.S. virtually 100 percent of such funding goes to the capital markets.

"In Europe you're probably somewhere between five and 10 percent of the financing being done in the capital markets." That could quickly jump to about 20 percent, he said, but growth after that would be slower.

In 1995, estimated municipal bond issuance was nearly $160 billion. That compared with some $465 billion of international bonds issued through the Eurobond market in that year, according to Euromoney Bondware data.
Maguire said there were a number of reasons why muni bond issuance has been slower to get going in Europe than the U.S.

For one thing, he said, competition among European banks is that much fiercer, making it easy for local entities to get financing directly from the banks. At the same time, the investment base for muni issues is different.
"In Europe the primary buyers of capital issuance are institutional investors. In the U.S. you have retail, or funds directed at retail investors," Maquire said.
He estimated about 75 percent of the market in the U.S. went to retail investors or their proxy.
"It will grow but it will grow relatively slowly. Clearly Italy has made a big push to put laws in place. There have been issuance in Spain. There's some level of issuance in France."
WHAT'S IN A NAME?

Once the currency risks are eliminated and tax implications are determined, investors will still have to grapple with the "name recognition" issue -- a factor that does not affect the more homogenous U.S. market so greatly.
Credit rating agencies will be one key to overcoming this obstacle, analysts said.
"It will be much more focused on actual credit and less on the advantage of name recognition," said Konrad Reuss, director of the sovereign group at Standard & Poor's in London.
"It will just be a much bigger and more transparent market than the domestic markets are right now."
He said that by removing currency risk for many investors, EMU will enlarge the pool of potential muni bond investors.
"Going forward, whether you invest in a Swedish municipality or German Laender (regions) or a French region, this issue isn't there anymore," Reuss said.
Lehman's Fox added, "The potential range of buyers for any specific cities changes dramatically. There's no reason why an Italian mutual fund shouldn't buy a bond issued by a UK city."

These prospects, of course, hinge on whether countries such as Britain and Sweden take part in EMU. Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg and Austria are all considered likely candidates for a single currency, due to start in 1999.

Finland and Ireland are also considered possibly early entrants, while Italy, Spain and Portugal are committed to EMU but markets are not sure whether they will be in at the start or later, analysts say.
